name: Lettuce
summary: How Filipino farmers usually grow litsugas from seedlings on raised, mulched beds, the Benguet way, from sowing in a seedbed to cutting the heads or leaves about two months after transplanting. For highland growers and lowland farmers who plant it in the cool months, with the changes that give cleaner, heavier lettuce.
season: In the highlands, such as La Trinidad, Atok and Buguias in Benguet, the Bukidnon uplands and the Cebu highlands, lettuce is grown all year, with rain shelters in the wettest months. In the lowlands it is grown in the cool dry months, mostly the loose leaf types, with light shade in hot weather.
material: Seed, only about 150 to 200 g a hectare. Farmers soak the seed in warm water for a few hours, air dry it, and sow it thinly in seedbeds. Seedlings are pricked out once, hardened, and transplanted.
spacing: Raised beds about 1 m wide with 75 cm paths. Holes 30 to 40 cm apart, two rows a bed for head types and three rows for leaf types. One seedling a hole.
water: Seedbeds are watered daily. The field by sprinkler, hose or furrow, keeping the soil evenly moist. Mulch keeps the leaves clean and the soil from drying or splashing. Standing water brings rot.
fertilizer: Beds get rotted chicken manure, about 1 kg a square meter, and carbonized rice hull before transplanting. At transplanting a little 14 14 14 goes in each hole, then urea, with potash for head lettuce, at about 15 and 30 days. Many highland growers also water with manure tea or fermented plant juice.
care: Pricking and hardening of seedlings, raised beds under straw or plastic mulch, regular watering, one or two small side dressings, and close watch for loopers, aphids and rot.
harvest: Leaf lettuce is cut from about a month after transplanting, before it bolts. Head lettuce at about 45 to 60 days, when the heads are firm. Farmers cut early in the morning, sort in the field and pack in boxes with holes, kept cool on the way to market.

ways.label: Seedbed, pricking, then mulched beds (punla at lipat tanim)

steps.title: Sow in the seedbed
steps.how: Make seedbeds about 1 by 10 m, mix in rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull, wet the bed and draw shallow lines 7 to 10 cm apart. Sow the soaked seed thinly, cover lightly and mulch with rice hull or chopped straw.

parts.title: Soak the seed, then air dry it
parts.how: Soak the seed in warm water for a few hours so it sprouts quickly and evenly. Spread it on paper or a cloth in the shade to dry a little, so the tiny seeds do not stick together in the hand.

parts.title: Ready the beds
parts.how: For one hectare of lettuce, about five seedbeds of 1 by 10 m are enough. Crush the soil fine and mix in about 1 kg of rotted chicken manure and 300 grams of carbonized rice hull for every square meter.

parts.title: Clean the soil if you can
parts.how: Some growers wet the seedbed with wood vinegar or a homemade microbe mix before sowing to keep down the fungi that kill young seedlings.

parts.title: Wet the bed and sow in lines
parts.how: Water the bed first, then draw shallow lines across it about 7 to 10 cm apart. Sprinkle the seed thinly along the lines and cover it with only a light dusting of soil.

parts.title: Mulch and water daily
parts.how: Cover the lines thinly with coir fiber, fine rice hull or straw chopped short to keep the top moist, and water every day with a fine sprinkler can.

steps.title: Prick out the seedlings
steps.how: At the two leaf stage, about two weeks after sowing, move the seedlings to another bed or to trays so each has room. Give light shade in hot weather and a plastic roof in the rains.

parts.title: Wait for two leaves
parts.how: Prick the seedlings when they show their first two leaves, about two weeks after sowing.

parts.title: Fill the trays
parts.how: Fill nursery trays or another bed with a loose mix that has vermicompost in it. The rich, soft mix helps the moved seedlings recover quickly.

parts.title: Move one seedling a cell
parts.how: Lift the seedlings with a little soil on the roots, holding them by a leaf, and set one in each tray cell. Firm the mix around it and water gently.

parts.title: Shade in the dry months, roof in the rains
parts.how: Keep the trays under light shade in the hot season and under a plastic roof in the rainy season, and water every day. They go to the field about three weeks after pricking.

steps.title: Plow and harrow twice
steps.how: Plow and harrow the field two times until the soil is fine.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: In the last week, water less often and give the seedlings full sun so they do not wilt after transplanting.

steps.title: Raise and mulch the beds
steps.how: Form raised beds about 1 m wide with 75 cm paths. Mix rotted chicken manure and carbonized rice hull into the bed, cover it with rice straw or plastic mulch, and punch holes 30 to 40 cm apart: two rows for head types, three rows for leaf types.

steps.title: Transplant in the afternoon
steps.how: Water the holes, put a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in each, then set one seedling a hole and press the soil around it. Replace any that die right away.

steps.title: Keep the beds moist
steps.how: Water regularly, enough to keep the soil damp but never soggy.

steps.title: First side dressing
steps.how: Give each plant a small pinch of urea, mixed half and half with muriate of potash (0 0 60) for head lettuce. Leaf lettuce needs only this one urea feeding.

steps.title: Scout for loopers and rot
steps.how: Look for green loopers and aphids under the leaves and for soft, slimy rot at the base. Remove rotting plants.

steps.title: Second side dressing for head lettuce
steps.how: Head lettuce gets a second small feeding of urea and potash about a month after transplanting.

steps.title: Sort and pack cool
steps.how: Sort in the field, pack in boxes with holes, and keep them cool and shaded until they reach the buyer.

steps.title: Harvest early in the morning
steps.how: Cut leaf lettuce when it reaches market size and before it bolts. Head lettuce is cut when the heads are firm, about 45 to 60 days after transplanting. Harvest early so the leaves do not wilt.

mistakes: Transplanting soft seedlings that were never hardened, so many wilt.
Planting head types in the hot lowland months, so they bolt and turn bitter.
Leaving the beds bare, so rain splashes soil on the leaves and rot sets in.
Too much urea late in the crop, which gives soft, quick rotting leaves.
Harvesting at midday or packing in closed sacks.
better: Choose varieties for your elevation and season, with heat tolerant leaf types for the lowlands.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with compost or rotted manure plus small, timed side dressings.
Raise seedlings under a rain shelter and harden them a week before transplanting.
Use raised, mulched beds and sun the prepared beds for a week to reduce rot.
Scout weekly and keep the plants cool from harvest to market.

watering.traditional: Lettuce seedlings are watered every day, and in the field growers water right after transplanting and then every day or regularly by sprinkler, hose or furrow, keeping the soil evenly moist. In the highlands many beds are mulched and watered from springs by hose or sprinkler. In the lowlands it is grown in the cool dry months near water.
watering.method: Sprinklers and hoses fed from springs in the highlands, and watering cans, hoses or furrows in the lowlands. Water early in the morning at the base so the leaves dry before night.
watering.rainfed: Lettuce is not grown on rain alone: it needs water almost every day. In the wettest highland months growers use rain shelters, and in the lowlands it goes in the cool dry months near a well or canal, with mulch on the beds.
watering.dryseason: Water every day in dry weather, more on sandy soil and in wind, early in the morning. Water when the top soil under the mulch is dry to the touch or the outer leaves go limp by mid morning.
watering.wet: Use raised, mulched beds and rain shelters in the wettest months, and skip watering when the beds are wet. Standing water and wet heads bring soft rot and leaf spots.

schedule.often: Water the bed before sowing, then every day in the morning
schedule.amount: A fine spray that keeps the top soil damp
schedule.why: Lettuce seed is tiny and sits at the surface, and it dies if the top soil dries.

schedule.often: Water every day after pricking out, under light shade in hot weather
schedule.why: Young seedlings rot at the base in soggy trays or beds.

schedule.often: Water less often while the seedlings get full sun
schedule.why: Hardened seedlings wilt less after transplanting.

schedule.often: Water the beds and the planting holes well before setting the seedlings, then water right after
schedule.why: Moist soil around the roots lets the seedlings settle overnight.

schedule.often: Every day in dry weather, by sprinkler, hose or furrow, in the morning
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the soil damp but never soggy
schedule.why: Lettuce has short roots and grows fast and tender only with steady moisture.

schedule.stage: Heading or full leaf to harvest
schedule.often: Keep watering daily or every other day. Water at the base and in the morning
schedule.why: Dry days turn the leaves bitter and make the plant bolt, while wet heads rot from the inside.

critical: The seedbed, where the top soil must never dry.
The whole field growth: even a few dry days make bitter leaves and early bolting.

signs.dry: Outer leaves wilt and their edges brown, the leaves turn tough and bitter, and the plants bolt early.
signs.wet: Lower leaves yellow and rot, heads go soft and slimy at the base, and seedlings fall over at the soil line.

better: Mulch the beds with plastic or rice straw to keep the soil evenly moist and the leaves clean of splashed mud.
A drip line or a fine sprinkler on a timer gives the steady daily water lettuce needs with less work.
